brief.head: Being right matters
brief.text: Ajay Shah has no in­ter­est in sol­i­dar­ity or being in a gang. What mat­ters, he said, is the minor mat­ter of being cor­rect: fore­cast­ing what an in­ter­ven­tion will do. {107-C04}

brief.head: Power keeps itself
brief.text: Asked by Ajay Shah why state own­er­ship ends in one-party rule, Amit Varma, think­ing aloud, said power seized by co­er­cion is kept by co­er­cion. {107-C16}

brief.head: Woke, then and now
brief.text: ‘Woke’ once meant awake to so­cial in­jus­tice, a sense Amit Varma em­braces. As an ide­ol­ogy, he ar­gued, it suc­ceeds Marxism: “wokeism be­gins where lib­er­al­ism ends.” {107-C23}

brief.head: Off the record
brief.text: An openly left-wing American aca­demic asked Amit Varma not to raise wokeism on the show. He would rant off the record, he said, but not on it. {107-S12}

brief.head: Proud no longer
brief.text: A dear friend of both hosts dropped “a proud right winger” from his Twitter bio about eleven or twelve years ago, once the word’s mean­ing had changed. {107-S11}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the labels we hurl
lead.head: Lifting the fog of the isms

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 107

body: Liberal, con­ser­va­tive, so­cial­ist, na­tion­al­ist, left, right: the la­bels are hurled around daily, and they mean dif­fer­ent things to dif­fer­ent peo­ple. On pop­u­lar de­mand, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah set out to de­fine them.
Shah promised lis­ten­ers “a beau­ti­ful sto­ry­line”. Varma replied that there was one way in which Shah was like a so­cial­ist: “you prom­ise a lot.”
They would be as neu­tral as they could, they said, though nei­ther uses any of these la­bels now. Labels, they warned, are dan­ger­ous.
## Three warn­ings

First, sep­a­rate the com­mon noun from the proper noun: a word’s dic­tio­nary mean­ing is one thing, the bag­gage a label ac­quires an­other. “I know many na­tion­al­ists who in my view are anti-national,” Varma said. {107-C01}
Second, la­bels move. ‘Liberal’ in Europe today means al­most the op­po­site of what it means in the US.

Third, la­bels come with tribes. People who join one adopt all its dog­mas and fol­low it wher­ever it drifts, as so many American con­ser­va­tives and lib­er­tar­i­ans fol­lowed Trump. Varma saw the same, to a dif­fer­ent ex­tent, in India.

Hence Varma’s fifth law: “All la­bels that be­stow any kind of pres­tige or virtue upon the bearer even­tu­ally come to mean the op­po­site, as grifters and op­por­tunists out­num­ber the be­liev­ers.” {107-C02}
Did Shah know the first four laws? “No, not even one.” Nor, Varma ad­mit­ted, did he.
Shah added that an idea is not re­spon­si­ble for the per­son who be­lieves in it: if Trump be­lieves some­thing, that says noth­ing about whether it is true.
## What they be­lieve

Before defin­ing any­thing, Varma set out the two hosts’ shared be­liefs. The world is pos­i­tive-sum. Top-down de­sign fails at the scale of a so­ci­ety. Actions must be judged by out­comes, not in­ten­tions. And free­dom is good in it­self and de­liv­ers the best out­comes, so think in terms of in­di­vid­u­als, not groups.

Shah’s il­lus­tra­tion of out­comes over in­ten­tions was Adolf Hitler: “if your ob­jec­tive was the glory and fur­ther­ance of the Germanic peo­ples, of German DNA, then there was no big­ger dis­as­ter for that than the man who es­poused this the most.” {107-C05}
## From Locke to Kling

Then came the la­bels, one by one. Liberalism, Varma said, be­gins with John Locke’s idea that we own our­selves. Conservatism, in its so­phis­ti­cated form, be­gins with Edmund Burke’s warn­ing that means mat­ter.
Marxism, so­cial­ism and com­mu­nism are a the­ory, a path and a des­ti­na­tion. Statism is less an ide­ol­ogy than an at­ti­tude: that so­ci­ety can be run from the top.
Varma quoted David Boaz: con­ser­va­tives want to be your daddy, lib­er­als want to be your mommy, and lib­er­tar­i­ans want to treat you as an adult.

Left and right began as seat­ing in the French National Assembly. In India, Varma said, they make no sense: “All our par­ties are left of cen­tre when it comes to eco­nom­ics and right of cen­ter in a bad way when it comes to so­ci­ety.” {107-C19}

He closed with Arnold Kling’s *The Three Languages of Politics*. Progressives argue from equal­ity, lib­er­tar­i­ans from free­dom and con­ser­va­tives from tra­di­tion, so they talk past each other. {107-C24}
The way out is to grant the other side’s val­ues. If both of you want less poverty, argue from his­tory and ev­i­dence about what will de­liver it, and minds can change.
Better still, Varma ad­vised, don’t pin la­bels on the other per­son at all: “Instead talk about prin­ci­ples, talk about val­ues.”

second.label: The man of system
second.head: Sparrows out, locusts in
second.deck: Amit Varma’s classic illustration of what top-down planning can do
body: In 1958 farm­ers in China com­plained that spar­rows were both­er­ing them. Chairman Mao de­cided that all spar­rows should be put to death, and wher­ever they could be caught across China, they were killed. {#sparrows}

But spar­rows ate lo­custs, Amit Varma said. Once the spar­rows died out, the lo­custs pro­lif­er­ated and de­stroyed China’s crops. A great famine fol­lowed in which forty-five mil­lion peo­ple died, in what is known as the Great Leap Forward. {107-S01}

For Varma it is the clas­sic il­lus­tra­tion of Adam Smith’s “man of sys­tem”, who imag­ines he can ar­range peo­ple like pieces on a chess­board. Society is too com­plex for that, he said. Respect the com­plex­ity, and don’t med­dle too much.

quote.text: When the spar­rows died out, the lo­custs pro­lif­er­ated and they de­stroyed all the crops of China.

third.head: Tiki-taka was a taunt

pic.caption: Amit Varma on how tiki-taka began as an insult

body: Tiki-taka is now the name for Pep Guardiola’s pos­ses­sion foot­ball, which comes from Johan Cruyff’s Total Football. But Guardiola hates the term, Amit Varma said. He didn’t coin it. {107-S06}

The broad­caster Andrés Montes first used it dur­ing the 2006 World Cup, be­fore Guardiola was a coach, to de­scribe Spain’s point­less pass­ing. Javier Clemente, the coach of Athletic Bilbao, used it the same dis­mis­sive way. Only later did it at­tach it­self to Barcelona.
Varma’s point was about pol­i­tics. ‘Liberal’ began as a pe­jo­ra­tive, and ‘conservative’ was first used as a cuss word against Edmund Burke, who did not coin it ei­ther.

Philosophical ge­niuses, Varma said, are den­i­grated and kicked about, in eco­nom­ics as in foot­ball. “Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman, Pep Guardiola, these are all ge­niuses,” he said, “and we should re­spect and ven­er­ate them.” {107-J12}

box.title: Adam Smith, read aloud
box.text: Amit Varma read Adam Smith aloud twice: on the “man of sys­tem”, and on how “peace, easy taxes, and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice” carry a state to op­u­lence. Smith, he said, prob­a­bly first used ‘liberal’ po­lit­i­cally. {107-J16}

sections.label: Liberal
sections.head: Liberal with the definitions
sections.caption: the great liberal paradox
body: ‘Liberal’ comes from the Latin *liber* or *liberalis*, mean­ing gen­er­ous and be­fit­ting a free per­son, Amit Varma said. Hence a man who gives too freely is “lib­eral with his wealth”. {107-J14}

The fa­ther of lib­er­al­ism, he said, is John Locke, whose foun­da­tional right is self-ownership. From it fol­low the rights to life, free speech and prop­erty. Isaiah Berlin later called these neg­a­tive rights.

Mary Wollstonecraft, one of Varma’s great he­roes, read Locke at the end of the 18th cen­tury and drew the next con­clu­sion: if all of us have these rights, women have them too. Modern fem­i­nism, he said, grew out of that. {107-S08}
## A nec­es­sary evil

Rights need some­one to en­force them. Hence the state, which Thomas Paine, in *Common Sense*, called a nec­es­sary evil. It is evil, Varma said, be­cause it holds a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence and lives on co­erced taxes: to pro­tect our rights, we must give up some of them. {107-C07}
Every ide­ol­ogy, in his view, is re­ally an ar­gu­ment about how much state vi­o­lence is jus­ti­fied.

Europe kept the older mean­ing of lib­eral. In 20th-century America, lib­er­als took up pos­i­tive rights, like a right to food, and the night-watchman state be­came an all-encompassing *maibaap* that had to feed you and clothe you. {107-C08}

~ When ‘liberal’ changed in America, Ajay Shah sug­gested, the small-state peo­ple called them­selves lib­er­tar­ian, and Varma agreed. Most lib­er­tar­i­ans, he said, are re­ally just clas­si­cal lib­er­als.

quote.text: I call it the great lib­eral para­dox, that for our rights to have mean­ing we must give up some of them

sections.label: Conservative
sections.head: Conserve what, exactly?
sections.caption: Burke and why means matter
body: ‘Conservative’ comes from the Latin for con­serve or pre­serve, Amit Varma said, which raises the ques­tion: con­serve what? A monar­chy, Christian fam­ily val­ues, even free en­ter­prise against the wel­fare state.

The se­ri­ous phi­los­o­phy, for him, comes from Edmund Burke, whose *Reflections on the Revolution in France* granted the rev­o­lu­tion its fine in­ten­tions and warned that its means were all wrong. {107-R14}

Institutions and norms, Varma said, “have gone through nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, they’ve passed the test of time”. Change the world by all means, but you can­not burn ev­ery­thing to the ground. {107-C10}
## Two im­pulses

Ajay Shah sep­a­rated two im­pulses in the word. One pre­serves an es­tab­lished order: re­li­gion, fam­ily, a so­cial struc­ture, an oli­garchy. The other re­spects the com­plex­ity of the world, mis­trusts grand schemes and holds that means mat­ter. {107-C09}
Varma re­jected the first, be­cause the world needs rad­i­cal change, and signed on com­pletely to the sec­ond.
His he­roes of the free­dom strug­gle were the mod­er­ates, such as Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale: lib­eral in their ends, con­ser­va­tive in their means. {107-S05}

~ India, he ar­gued, has lit­tle Burkean con­ser­vatism. Much of what goes by the name pre­serves the past for its own sake, or is a rad­i­cal trib­al­ism at odds with India’s as­sim­ila­tive tra­di­tions.

quote.text: It’s a re­spect for the rich­ness and com­plex­ity of the world. It’s a mis­trust of any grand scheme.

sections.label: Marxism
sections.head: Great idea, wrong species
sections.caption: theory, path and destination
body: Marxism, so­cial­ism and com­mu­nism be­long to­gether but mean sub­tly dif­fer­ent things. “You can think of Marxism as a the­ory, so­cial­ism as a path, com­mu­nism as a des­ti­na­tion,” Amit Varma said. {107-C11}

From the *Communist Manifesto* of 1848 and *Das Kapital* of 1867 came a world of two classes: a bour­geoisie own­ing the means of pro­duc­tion and a pro­le­tariat it ex­ploits. Revolution would bring a dic­ta­tor­ship of the pro­le­tariat.

Such a the­ory seems to ex­plain ev­ery­thing, which is why it se­duces the young. At eigh­teen Varma car­ried *Das Kapital* in his col­lege bag for a few days, feel­ing cool and in­tel­lec­tual. {107-S09}
## Five charges

It re­duces ev­ery­thing to class, said Max Weber and Karl Popper. Capitalism never col­lapsed, said Popper and Fukuyama. It ig­nores race and gen­der, said Michel Foucault and in­ter­sec­tional thinkers, and in India, Varma added, caste. It de­fies human na­ture, said Isaiah Berlin. And it needs mass vi­o­lence, said Hannah Arendt and Raymond Aron.
The bi­ol­o­gist E.O. Wilson put it as “Great idea, wrong species”: it would work for ants. {107-J03}
Ajay Shah of­fered a Soviet joke. You must break eggs to make an omelette, ran the ex­cuse, until some­one asked: “We broke a lot of eggs. Where’s the omelette?” {107-J04}
~ Booms and busts are nor­mal, Shah said, and small be­side the com­pound­ing of growth: “when you cor­rectly draw the graph, the fluc­tu­a­tions ap­pear ir­rel­e­vant.” {107-C13}

quote.text: any ide­o­log­i­cal the­ory that works will ap­pear to ex­plain ev­ery­thing and there­fore is deeply se­duc­tive to the young.

sections.label: Socialism
sections.head: Good for society? Not quite
sections.caption: what ‘socialist’ really means
body: In India, Amit Varma said, so­cial­ism is used al­most be­nignly, as if it meant what­ever is good for so­ci­ety. In po­lit­i­cal sci­ence it means some­thing spe­cific.
He gave four fea­tures: pub­lic own­er­ship of re­sources, re­dis­tri­bu­tion to bring about equal out­comes, a planned econ­omy, and fine in­ten­tions that so­cial­ism never achieves.
Jawaharlal Nehru, under the sway of the Fabian Society he en­coun­tered in England, was a Fabian so­cial­ist, and India got its five-year plans. {107-J18}
## The wrong pre­am­ble

Varma op­posed the CAA, which he called mon­strous, and was de­lighted to see young peo­ple march hold­ing the Preamble. But many car­ried the amended text with ‘socialist’ in it, not Ambedkar’s orig­i­nal. {107-S03}
“Socialist doesn’t mean what is good for so­ci­ety,” he said. “Socialism kept us poor for decades longer than nec­es­sary.” {107-C15}
Ajay Shah had pointed out that the Hindi *samajwad* car­ries none of the bag­gage of pub­lic own­er­ship: it broadly means on the side of so­ci­ety. In that sense, Varma said, he is one.
Shah wished Ambedkar, in keep­ing ‘socialist’ out, had added that the only way to make a so­cial­ism is to crush in­di­vid­ual rights, which can­not go with con­sti­tu­tional lib­eral democ­racy.
~ Varma ob­jected on Ambedkar’s be­half. History had not played out, the Soviet Union still seemed a suc­cess, and caste, a vis­ceral evil, oc­cu­pied his at­ten­tion.

quote.text: many of them were hold­ing the wrong pre­am­ble. They were not hold­ing Ambedkar’s pre­am­ble, they were hold­ing Indira’s pre­am­ble

sections.label: Nationalism
sections.head: Anti-national, by Varma’s law
sections.caption: patriots and nationalists
body: Both hosts love their coun­try deeply and hate na­tion­al­ism deeply, Amit Varma said. Patriotism is lov­ing your coun­try. Nationalism de­fines a na­tion by oth­er­ing some peo­ple, play­ing on tribal in­stincts hard­wired into us.

He cited Tagore, who called na­tion­al­ism a great men­ace, and Karl Popper, who wrote in *The Open Society and Its Enemies* that it ap­peals to our tribal in­stincts, “to pas­sion and to prej­u­dice”. {107-R15}

Savarkar’s *What is Hindutva*, which Varma dated to 1925, de­fined a Hindu as some­one whose home­land and land of wor­ship are both India. That takes in Jains and Buddhists and shuts out Muslims and Christians. Varma called it mas­ter­ful and deeply toxic. {107-C21}
## Varma’s sixth law
Varma quoted Ramachandra Guha: a pa­triot strives for a less vi­o­lent, less poor, less ex­ploita­tive coun­try, while “a na­tion­al­ist wants to bomb ev­ery­body else”. {107-C20}
Hence his pro­posed sixth law: any­one who calls oth­ers anti-national is the true anti-national.

Ajay Shah ad­mired how Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru were Indian and open to the world at once; Gandhi, he noted, read the New Testament with great in­ter­est. Nationalism in India, Shah said, stems from deep in­se­cu­rity. {107-C22}
~ Nitin Pai, whom both hosts ad­mire, ar­gues for lib­eral na­tion­al­ism. Varma, who ar­gued against it at length with Pai on his show, al­lows that he may be wrong.

quote.text: If you’re ac­tu­ally strong, if you’re ac­tu­ally ca­pa­ble, then you will relax, then you will en­gage with oth­ers as equals

I know many lib­er­als who are not lib­eral. I know many pro­gres­sive peo­ple who es­pouse poli­cies that would ac­tu­ally set us back and not take us for­ward. I know many con­ser­va­tives who hold rad­i­cal views

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the word Ambedkar kept out of the Preamble
stories.head: Not in my preamble
body: In 1948, as the Constituent Assembly de­bated the Preamble, K.T. Shah moved to add three words to it. B.R. Ambedkar re­jected two of them: ‘secular’ and ‘socialist’.
His ob­jec­tion to ‘secular’, Amit Varma said, was not to sec­u­lar­ism. It was writ­ten into every ar­ti­cle of the Constitution al­ready, so spell­ing it out was un­nec­es­sary.

On ‘socialist’, Varma read out Ambedkar’s speech to the Assembly. A con­sti­tu­tion, Ambedkar said, “is merely a mech­a­nism for the pur­pose of reg­u­lat­ing the work of the var­i­ous or­gans of the state”. {#ambedkarspeech}

How so­ci­ety should be or­gan­ised, he said, must be de­cided by the peo­ple them­selves ac­cord­ing to time and cir­cum­stances. To fix it in the Constitution would be “de­stroy­ing democ­racy al­to­gether”. Thinking peo­ple might one day de­vise some­thing bet­ter than the so­cial­ist or­gan­i­sa­tion of today or to­mor­row.
The words went in any­way, added by Indira Gandhi in the mid-1970s. Today, Varma said, any po­lit­i­cal party that reg­is­ters in India must pledge al­le­giance to so­cial­ism.

Not that he and Ajay Shah plan a party, which, he said, “of course we never will, be­cause we are thinkers and not doers”. Then he cor­rected him­self: “No, we are doers but in a dif­fer­ent way.” {107-J08}
If they did, Varma said, they would have to pledge to so­cial­ism, “which fun­da­men­tally goes against ev­ery­thing we be­lieve in”. {107-S02}

~ S.V. Raju, the late pres­i­dent of the Swatantra Party, fought the rule in court for many years, ar­gu­ing that a party that stood against so­cial­ism could not pledge al­le­giance to it. It was, Varma said, a los­ing bat­tle.
stories.why: A con­sti­tu­tion, Ambedkar ar­gued, should reg­u­late the or­gans of the state and leave the peo­ple free to choose how so­ci­ety is or­gan­ised. Writing in one ide­ol­ogy took that choice away, and still de­cides who may enter pol­i­tics.
stories.postscript: Ambedkar’s col­lected writ­ings, sixty-plus vol­umes, and Gandhi’s ninety-nine are free on­line. “This stuff is free,” Varma said. {#ninetynine}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Ambedkar’s original preamble

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s invented correspondence, built from real quotes
stories.head: Bro, I warned you
body: In 1790, with the French Revolution under way, Edmund Burke wrote *Reflections on the Revolution in France*. {#burke} He did not quar­rel with its ideals of lib­erty, equal­ity and fra­ter­nity. He warned that its means were dis­as­trous.

For the History of Ideas we­bi­nar in their Life Lessons course, Amit Varma made up post­cards be­tween Burke and Robespierre, one of the no­table fig­ures be­hind the rev­o­lu­tion, built from the men’s real quotes.

In the first, Robespierre tells Burke, roughly, to shut up, calls him an old fogey and asks what he is even try­ing to con­serve. Burke’s reply: “Bro, I warned you, I hope you’re around to read this.” {107-S04}
~ Robespierre was not. He had him­self been purged, Varma said, after doing a fair amount of purg­ing.
stories.why: Ends and means are sep­a­rate ques­tions. Change the world by all means, Varma ar­gued, but in­sti­tu­tions and norms that have passed the test of time exist for a rea­son, and you can­not sim­ply burn them to the ground. {107-C10}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Burke’s postcard to Robespierre

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how land lost its hold on Indian wealth
stories.head: Ploughed under by Infosys
body: Think of the word land in India in 1907 or 1947, Ajay Shah said, and the pri­mal emo­tions around it. Land meant wealth and in­come, and the game was to own more of it.
“A per­son with fifty thou­sand acres was a big­ger per­son than a per­son with 10,000 acres,” he said. {107-S07}

Today’s India makes its wealth from busi­ness: you build Infosys, you build Reliance Industries. Land is nice to have, but nei­ther nec­es­sary nor suf­fi­cient to be rich, suc­cess­ful and im­por­tant.

~ Thinkers from Adam Smith to Karl Marx, Shah said, saw cap­i­tal­ism and glob­al­i­sa­tion as a wild west wind that would tear up the feu­dal order. {107-R16} Those who did well from land, aris­toc­racy, re­li­gion and fam­ily wanted the old order kept, which is how ‘conservative’ came to stand against ‘liberal’.

quote.text: The wealth of today’s India is not cre­ated out of land.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on land, wealth and the old order

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a slur that comes without a definition
stories.head: Define ‘neoliberal’. She couldn’t
body: Among the terms Amit Varma ran through at the end of the episode was ‘neoliberal’, which he called a pure cuss word used against peo­ple who are for mar­kets.
At the end of a re­ally great episode of his show *The Seen and the Unseen*, a guest used it. He chal­lenged her on it, and she couldn’t even de­fine it. {107-S10}

It was a slightly awk­ward bit of con­ver­sa­tion, he ad­mit­ted, and he won’t link the episode. Define the term, he told her, and then they could dis­cuss it: you can’t just use it as a pe­jo­ra­tive.

~ Now, when­ever he hears some­one use the word, his mind stops tak­ing them se­ri­ously. {#seriously} He sus­pects they have been brain­washed in some American uni­ver­sity sys­tem. “I live in the real world,” he said.
stories.why: If some­one can­not de­fine the label they use as an in­sult, the label is doing their think­ing. Asking the other side to de­fine its terms, as Varma did, is where a real ar­gu­ment be­gins.

quiz.a: Great idea, wrong species: his point was that it would work for ants.

quiz.q: How did Varma distinguish Marxism, socialism and communism in one line?
quiz.a: Marxism is a the­ory, so­cial­ism a path, com­mu­nism a des­ti­na­tion.

quiz.q: What happened after Mao ordered China’s sparrows killed in 1958, according to Varma?
quiz.a: Locusts mul­ti­plied, de­stroyed the crops, and forty-five mil­lion died in the famine.

quiz.q: In David Boaz’s quip, what do conservatives, liberals and libertarians each want?
quiz.a: To be your daddy, to be your mommy, and to treat you as an adult.

quiz.q: Who coined ‘tiki-taka’, and how was the term first meant?
quiz.a: The broad­caster Andrés Montes, at the 2006 World Cup, mock­ing Spain’s point­less pass­ing.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 107. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Mao Zedong (Chen Zhengqing (1917–1966), public domain); John Locke (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); Mary Wollstonecraft (John Opie, public domain); Edmund Burke (Joshua Reynolds, public domain); Karl Marx (John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain); Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); Rabindranath Tagore (Generalstabens litografiska anstalt, public domain); Karl Popper (Franz Barta, No restrictions); Thomas Sowell (Internet Archive Book Images, public domain); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Open Library.

shelf.title: The Three Languages of Politics
shelf.creator: Arnold Kling
shelf.why: A slim book you can read in an hour on why po­lit­i­cal dis­course is bro­ken: pro­gres­sives argue from equal­ity, con­ser­va­tives from tra­di­tion and lib­er­tar­i­ans from free­dom, so they talk past each other.

shelf.title: Communism
shelf.creator: Richard Pipes
shelf.why: A slim vol­ume on what ac­tu­ally hap­pened under com­mu­nism, link­ing ideas to ac­tions to con­se­quences.

shelf.title: The Libertarian Mind: A Manifesto for Freedom
shelf.creator: David Boaz
shelf.why: Boaz is one of Amit’s mod­ern he­roes, a great thinker who died re­cently.

shelf.title: A Conflict of Visions
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Explains how ide­olo­gies take shape and come into being.

shelf.title: Economic Facts and Fallacies
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Sowell names foun­da­tional eco­nomic fal­la­cies from which many other er­rors grow; Amit says he fin­ished it a much clearer thinker about eco­nom­ics.

shelf.title: Capitalism and Freedom
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Not an in­tro­duc­tory book, but Ajay says each chap­ter is ‘like an earthquake’ that shakes you into think­ing about the world; part of the foun­da­tional read­ing be­hind Amit’s un­der­stand­ing of mar­kets and free­dom.

shelf.title: Free to Choose
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman and Rose Friedman
shelf.why: The Friedmans’ case for vol­un­tary ex­change, which Amit uses to argue that cap­i­tal­ism means con­sent and is the op­po­site of crony­ism; a core text on his ‘rec­om­mend ev­ery­thing by Friedman’ list.

shelf.title: Free to Choose (TV series)
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: An ac­ces­si­ble, watch­able ver­sion of Friedman’s case for free­dom, and Amit’s ex­am­ple of last­ing work that be­comes a body of knowl­edge oth­ers build on, un­like the daily flow of tweets and col­umns.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Collected Works of Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: The writ­ings of ‘the man who re­ally turned me on to freedom’, as Amit puts it: Bastiat put com­plex eco­nomic ideas into sim­ple lan­guage with­out dumb­ing them down, and gives you a frame­work for see­ing the world.

shelf.title: Collected Writings of B.R. Ambedkar
shelf.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
shelf.why: More than sixty vol­umes of Ambedkar’s writ­ings and speeches, free on­line and ‘amaz­ing to read’.

shelf.title: Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
shelf.creator: Mahatma Gandhi
shelf.why: Ninety-nine vol­umes, free to read, in which you can watch a man en­gage with the world in writ­ing every day, with un­var­nished hon­esty, like a blog­ger of his time.

shelf.title: Annihilation of Caste
shelf.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
shelf.why: Amit calls it Ambedkar’s ‘great mas­ter­piece of a book’.

shelf.title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
shelf.creator: Edmund Burke
shelf.why: The found­ing text for the idea that means mat­ter.

shelf.title: The Open Society and Its Enemies
shelf.creator: Karl Popper
shelf.why: Source of Popper’s di­ag­no­sis that na­tion­al­ism ap­peals to tribal in­stinct and lets peo­ple es­cape the strain of in­di­vid­ual re­spon­si­bil­ity.

shelf.title: The Communist Manifesto
shelf.creator: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
shelf.why: Ajay re­jects its pre­scrip­tions but finds whole chunks ‘ab­so­lutely brilliant’ on how cap­i­tal­ism and glob­al­i­sa­tion would tear up the feu­dal order.

shelf.title: Why Nationalism
shelf.creator: Yael Tamir
shelf.why: A se­ri­ous schol­arly case for na­tion­al­ism.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Arnold Kling
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An audio com­pan­ion to the book.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Jerry Rao on Indian conservatism
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A lively dis­agree­ment in which Amit ar­gues that Burkean con­ser­vatism barely ex­ists in India.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Nitin Pai on liberal nationalism
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long-form de­bate in which Nitin Pai, whom both hosts ad­mire, de­fends ‘lib­eral nationalism’ and Amit ar­gues against it, on the ten­sion be­tween de­fend­ing a nation’s bor­ders and serv­ing its peo­ple.

shelf.title: Episode on Mary Wollstonecraft
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s short audio in­tro­duc­tion, made for Storytel, to Mary Wollstonecraft’s A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: how one of his great he­roes ex­tended Locke’s rights to women and so began mod­ern fem­i­nism.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on Populism
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Populism is not ‘what is popular’ but a dan­ger­ous pack­age of be­liefs and meth­ods, ris­ing world­wide along­side na­tion­al­ism, that works by in­vent­ing en­e­mies and sell­ing in­su­lar slo­gans like im­port sub­sti­tu­tion.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything Episodes 25 and 26 on the role of the state
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything Episode 10 on Freedom
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on four papers that changed the world
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

laughs.text: After Ajay prom­ises lis­ten­ers a ‘beau­ti­ful storyline’, Amit replies: ‘there is one way in which you are like a so­cial­ist. Which is that you prom­ise a lot. And I’m wor­ried if [I] can de­liver.’
Introducing Varma’s Fifth Law, Amit asks Ajay: ‘Do you know the first four laws?’ Ajay: ‘No, not even one.’ Amit: ‘Neither do I.’ He prom­ises to ‘fig­ure out three more in be­tween later’.

Amit imag­ines the bi­ol­o­gist E.O. Wilson telling Karl Marx, who died long be­fore Wilson was born: ‘dude, great freak­ing the­ory, man, but sell it to the ants.’ Then he adds that ants are al­ready like that, so you don’t need to sell them any­thing.
Ajay’s Soviet joke: they jus­ti­fied the de­struc­tion by say­ing you have to break eggs to make an omelette, and then some­one asks, ‘We broke a lot of eggs. Where’s the omelette?’

Ajay: ‘He who has not been a Marxist as a child has no heart. And he who is a Marxist as an adult has no brain.’ Amit scolds him for using ‘left’ be­fore they have de­fined it, telling him not to use words they haven’t ex­plained yet, ‘which ba­si­cally would mean don’t say anything’.

Ajay on human in­equal­ity: ‘Everybody is not born with an Elo of 2830... My Elo sucks and you just got to ac­cept this. We’re all dif­fer­ent. I’m not Magnus.’ Later Amit says that when they play chess the plan may work ‘even if you’re not 2830’.

Amit on com­mu­nism: he’d pre­sum­ably be al­lowed to keep his iPad, though the state could take it any time, ‘Except that there would be no iPad be­cause I would not be rich enough in a com­mu­nist so­ci­ety to buy an iPad un­less I was kind of run­ning the show.’
On being un­able to reg­is­ter a party with­out pledg­ing to so­cial­ism: ‘which of course we never will, be­cause we are thinkers and not doers. No, we are doers but in a dif­fer­ent way.’

On Bill Clinton’s sen­si­ble pro-market pres­i­dency: ‘One could say his per­sonal fail­ing was he was too lib­eral with his af­fec­tions, but leav­ing that aside.’ This calls back to the episode’s open­ing point about ‘lib­eral with her affections’ as a com­mon-noun usage.
Amit on doing a full episode about wokeism some­day: ‘after which I will get lynched and the show will end. So maybe that’s well into the fu­ture.’
After the tiki-taka story: ‘Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman, Pep Guardiola, these are all ge­niuses, and we should re­spect and ven­er­ate them.’

Etymology: ‘liberal’ comes from the Latin liber/lib­er­alis, mean­ing gen­er­ous and be­fit­ting a free per­son. That is the source of ev­ery­day phrases like ‘lib­eral with her affections’ or ‘lib­eral with his wealth’.
Hobbes’s ‘nasty, brutish and short’ and Thomas Paine’s de­scrip­tion of gov­ern­ment as ‘a nec­es­sary evil’ in Common Sense. Amit says Paine’s is where the phrase first comes from.

Adam Smith prob­a­bly first used ‘liberal’ in a po­lit­i­cal sense in The Wealth of Nations, writ­ing of ‘the lib­eral sys­tem of free ex­por­ta­tion and free importation’. Amit adds: ‘So glob­al­iza­tion Zindabad.’

Ajay crit­i­cises Subhas Chandra Bose, whom he de­scribes as an ICS top­per who ‘wanted to pick up guns and change the order’. He ar­gues that anti-colonial move­ments fought with guns left a legacy of vi­o­lence that ripped up their so­ci­eties.
Nehru was ‘under the sway’ of the Fabian Society, which he en­coun­tered in England, and so be­came a Fabian so­cial­ist, which led to India’s five-year plans.
